title: Completeness: why Banach spaces ask for it
summary: Cauchy sequences, what it means for a metric space to be complete, why completeness is intrinsic while closedness is not, and which theorems need it.

check.prompt: Give a normed space in which some absolutely convergent series has no sum, and justify both halves: that the series is absolutely convergent, and that no element of the space is its sum.
check.guidance: One answer: c_00, the finitely supported real sequences, with the sup norm, and the series Σ_{k≥1} 2^{−k} e_k (e_k the k-th unit sequence). It is absolutely convergent because Σ ‖2^{−k} e_k‖_∞ = Σ 2^{−k} = 1. Its partial sums s_n = (1/2, 1/4, …, 2^{−n}, 0, 0, …) converge in sup norm, inside the larger space ℓ^∞, to x = (2^{−k})_k, since ‖x − s_n‖_∞ = 2^{−(n+1)}. Limits in a metric space are unique and c_00 sits inside ℓ^∞ with the same norm, so if the series had a sum in c_00 it would be x; but x has infinitely many non-zero terms, so it is not in c_00. Hence the series has no sum in c_00, which is consistent with c_00 being incomplete.

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Author's own review of each claim: convergent implies Cauchy; the sequence of continuous ramps f_n is L¹-Cauchy with ‖f_m − f_n‖_1 ≤ 1/n for m > n because f_m − f_n vanishes outside [1/2, 1/2 + 1/n] and |f_m − f_n| ≤ 1; an L¹ limit that is continuous would equal 0 on [0,1/2) and 1 on (1/2,1], impossible; a subset of a complete metric space is complete exactly when it is closed; the c_00 example in the self-check.
